paras: The lynching of Isaac Fisher took place on Monday, July 25, 1881, when a crowd took Fisher, a Black blacksmith, from his guards at Satartia in Yazoo County, Mississippi, and hanged him from a tree outside the village. Fisher was accused of raping a young white woman and drowning her in a cistern two days earlier. Wire dispatches spread the case nationally under approving headlines.

Fisher worked as a blacksmith on the Brown and Dalton plantation, which the Vicksburg Commercial's correspondent placed six miles from Satartia and the Jackson Weekly Clarion about ten miles below it. According to these accounts, on Saturday morning, July 23, he seized Rosa Ertel (printed 'Rosa Eatle' elsewhere), a young white woman living with F. W. Dalton, assaulted her, and threw her into a cistern. Finding her standing in the shallow water, the papers said, he climbed down the chain and drowned her, then could not climb out.

Fisher's own account, as printed, was that he went into the cistern to save her after seeing her fall in. The Clarion said the facts it gave came from his confession, and the Commercial's correspondent also wrote that he confessed.

On Sunday, Esquire A. H. Montgomery empaneled a jury, and Dr. J. B. Taylor examined the body before it. The Vicksburg Herald and the Richland Beacon reported that Fisher had first been released and was arrested again once the examination showed an assault, while the Clarion said no arrest was made until Sunday because Dalton and Brown were away. That evening he was brought to Satartia, where a meeting of citizens, described by the Commercial as white and colored, 'decided he was guilty' but put off action until Monday morning.

A New Orleans Democrat dispatch said the assembled citizens had voted on hanging him, but a majority chose to wait for the inquest. Early Monday a crowd gathered in town, and at half past nine a column of men overpowered the guards at the house where Fisher was held and led him out. He was hanged from a pecan tree about ten feet from the roadside, just outside the village, and the body hung there until two o'clock. The Commercial's correspondent put the crowd at about 300 and wrote that 'the surrounding country, both black and white' carried out the hanging; the Herald counted two or three hundred.
After the body was lowered, a coroner's jury returned a verdict that Fisher 'came to his death by hanging'. No report of an arrest or prosecution of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage.

The first word came in a Memphis Avalanche special from Yazoo City dated July 25, which said the 'demon was summarily dealt with' and joked that he was now taking 'a chat' with a man hanged the previous Thursday. Papers from Sacramento and Cheyenne to St. Paul and Pascagoula printed it on July 26-29 under headlines such as 'A Fiendish Act Promptly Punished', 'Just Retribution' and 'Served Him Right'. A Canton, Mississippi, version had 'infuriated people' hang Fisher as soon as he was drawn from the cistern and jested about the 'prevalent complaint—neck dislocation'.

A rival New Orleans Democrat dispatch, describing the vote to wait for an inquest, ran in the Knoxville Daily Chronicle under the headline 'A Case Where the Minority Should Have Ruled?' The Vicksburg Herald expected that 'the wretch has met a deserved death at the hands of Judge Lynch', and Mississippi weeklies later headed fuller accounts 'The Murderer Hung' and 'Judge Lanch Tries His Hand on a Negro Brute'. The Panola Star, in mid-August, listed Fisher as 'justly lynched'.

The one dissent came from the Osceola Times in Arkansas, which noted that the Avalanche had printed an editorial calling lynch law 'anarchy' directly above a 'Retribution' account of this case, written as if 'heroic treatment is sometimes necessary to the suppression of crime'.

Accounts differ on when Fisher was killed: the Avalanche dispatch implied he was hanged on discovery Saturday, and the Panola Star dated the lynching to the 23d, but the Satartia and Jackson accounts, written closer to the scene and in more detail, place it on Monday after the inquest.

Fisher was hanged without trial by a crowd that overpowered his guards, after a citizens' meeting 'decided he was guilty' of rape and murder (A17, A18); papers called it the work of 'Judge Lynch' (A6, A18).

Separate Vicksburg Herald, Vicksburg Commercial and Jackson Clarion accounts agree that Fisher was hanged near Satartia on Monday before a crowd (A6, A17, A18), and wire dispatches from Yazoo City report the lynching (A1, A12).

accounts.label: Memphis Avalanche Yazoo City special
accounts.gist: Fisher was found caged in the cistern, drawn out by gathering neighbors and hanged at once with 'a rope and a convenient limb'.

accounts.label: New Orleans Democrat Yazoo City special
accounts.gist: Assembled citizens voted on hanging Fisher, but the majority chose to hold him until an inquest.

accounts.label: Vicksburg Herald
accounts.gist: Fisher, first freed, was re-arrested; the crowd agreed to hang him after the inquest, and he was hanged Monday before two or three hundred people.

accounts.label: Vicksburg Commercial correspondent at Satartia
accounts.gist: After a Sunday inquest and a meeting of white and colored citizens, 'the surrounding country, both black and white' hanged Fisher about 10 a.m. Monday on a tree outside the village before about 300 people.

accounts.label: Jackson Weekly Clarion
accounts.gist: A citizens' meeting found him guilty Sunday night; Monday at 9:30 a column of men overpowered his guards and hanged him from a pecan tree by the road.

accounts.label: Fisher's own statement
accounts.gist: Fisher said he went into the cistern to save the girl after seeing her fall in; the Clarion and Commercial say he later confessed.

framing.detail: The Avalanche dispatch ran under 'A Fiendish Act Promptly Punished', 'Just Retribution' and 'Served Him Right', called Fisher 'the demon' and joked he was taking 'a chat' with a man hanged the week before.
The Canton American Citizen headed it 'A Horrid Deed Committed by a Negro' and jested about the 'prevalent complaint—neck dislocation'.
The Knoxville Daily Chronicle headed the New Orleans Democrat dispatch 'A Case Where the Minority Should Have Ruled?'
The Vicksburg Herald, via the Brookhaven Ledger, said 'the wretch has met a deserved death at the hands of Judge Lynch'; the Richland Beacon spoke of 'the punishment he deserved'.
The Osceola Times editorial 'Consistency' charged the Avalanche with condemning lynch law in one column while describing this hanging approvingly in the next.

Mississippi weeklies headlined 'The Outrage and Murder of a White Girl in Yazoo by a Negro Brute. The Murderer Hung' and 'Judge Lanch Tries His Hand on a Negro Brute', and called him 'justly lynched'.
A Minnesota crime roundup said only that the unnamed man was 'summarily lynched'.

record_check.dossier: One man, Isaac Fisher; 'Isaac Fish' (and 'Isiah', 'Isaiah') are spelling variants.
One person was killed by the mob (Fisher); the second death is Rosa Ertel's, the alleged crime that preceded the lynching.
Supported: hanged Monday, July 25; the alleged crime was Saturday, July 23.
Unnamed crowd; one account says 'both black and white' took part.
At least 12 white papers opened, plus further wire reprints, July 26 to August 13.

From a tree (a pecan, about ten feet from the roadside) just outside the village of Satartia; the alleged crime was at the Brown and Dalton plantation, six (or ten) miles from Satartia
Isaac Fisher (also printed 'Isiah', 'Isaiah', 'Issac' Fisher and 'Isaac Fish'), Black, a blacksmith on the plantation
Accused of raping a young white woman, Rosa Ertel (or Eatle), throwing her into a cistern and drowning her; he said he went into the cistern to save her
